definition: The set Ω of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
A subset of the sample space; it occurs when the outcome lies in it.
Non-negativity, P(Ω) = 1 and countable additivity: the three axioms that define a probability measure.
The formula for the probability of a union: add single events, subtract pairwise intersections, add triples, and so on.
P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ …) ≤ P(A₁) + P(A₂) + …, whatever the dependence (Boole's inequality).
C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!), the number of ways to choose k items from n without regard to order.
The surprisingly high chance of a shared birthday in a small group: over 50% with 23 people.
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B): the probability of A once B is known to have occurred.
P(A) = Σ P(A | Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ) over a partition B₁, B₂, …: split by cases and weight.
A game-show puzzle in which switching doors wins with probability 2/3, because the host's choice carries information.
Events with P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); for several events the product rule must hold for every subcollection.
P(H | E) = P(E | H)P(H)/P(E): converts the probability of evidence given a hypothesis into the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence.
Ignoring the prior probability of a hypothesis when judging evidence, as when most positive tests for a rare condition are false.
P(E | H)/P(E | not H): the factor by which evidence multiplies the odds of a hypothesis.
A numerical quantity determined by the outcome of an experiment; formally a measurable function on the sample space.
For a discrete random variable, p(x) = P(X = x).
F(x) = P(X ≤ x); non-decreasing, right-continuous, from 0 to 1. Defined for every random variable.
The random variable that is 1 when an event occurs and 0 otherwise; its mean is the event's probability.
A non-negative function whose integral over a set gives the probability of landing in it; not itself a probability.
The value below which a given fraction of the probability lies; the median is the 0.5-quantile.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable, E[X].
E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y] for any random variables with finite means, dependent or not.
E[g(X)] = Σ g(x)p(x) or ∫ g(x)f(x)dx: no need to find the distribution of g(X).
The mean squared deviation from the mean, E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − (E[X])².
The square root of the variance, in the same units as the variable.
The standardised third central moment; positive when the right tail is longer.
The standardised fourth central moment, a measure of tail weight; 3 for the normal ('excess kurtosis' subtracts 3).
Generating a sample with CDF F by applying the quantile function F⁻¹ to a uniform random number.
The number of successes in n independent trials with success probability p; mean np, variance np(1 − p).
The number of trials until the first success in independent trials; mean 1/p and memoryless.
A single trial: 1 with probability p, 0 otherwise.
Counts of rare events: P(N = k) = e^{−λ}λᵏ/k!, with mean and variance both λ.
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t): waiting so far tells you nothing about the remaining wait. Holds for the geometric and exponential distributions.
The waiting time to the first event at constant rate λ: density λe^{−λx}, mean 1/λ.
Waiting time to the k-th event of a Poisson process; shape k and rate λ, mean k/λ.
The bell-shaped distribution N(μ, σ²), the limit of standardised sums by the central limit theorem.
Converting X to (X − μ)/σ, which has mean 0 and variance 1.
The sum of squares of k independent standard normals; mean k, variance 2k.
Z/√(Q/ν) for a standard normal Z and an independent chi-square Q with ν degrees of freedom; heavier-tailed than the normal.
A family on [0, 1] with density proportional to x^{a−1}(1 − x)^{b−1}; models proportions and is the conjugate prior for a binomial probability.
The distribution of several random variables together, from which marginals and conditionals follow.
The distribution of one variable obtained by summing or integrating the joint distribution over the others.
E[(X − E X)(Y − E Y)]: how two variables move together linearly.
Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), between −1 and 1; measures linear association only.
The matrix of covariances of a random vector; symmetric and positive semidefinite.
E[Y | X], the best prediction of Y from X in mean square; itself a random variable.
Var(Y) = E[Var(Y | X)] + Var(E[Y | X]).
E[Y] = E[E[Y | X]], the tower property.
The distribution of a sum of independent random variables, computed by summing or integrating over the ways to make the total.
A random vector all of whose linear combinations are normal; fixed by its mean vector and covariance matrix.
G(s) = E[sˣ] for a non-negative integer variable; products of PGFs correspond to sums of independent variables.
M(t) = E[e^{tX}]; its derivatives at 0 are the moments.
φ(t) = E[e^{itX}], the Fourier transform of a distribution; always exists and determines it.
P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a for a non-negative X.
P(|X − μ| ≥ k) ≤ Var(X)/k².
An exponential bound on how far a mean of independent bounded variables strays from its expectation: P(X̄ − μ ≥ ε) ≤ exp(−2nε²/(b − a)²).
A tail bound obtained by applying Markov's inequality to e^{tX} and optimising over t.
g(E[X]) ≤ E[g(X)] for convex g (reversed for concave g).
H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x): the average uncertainty of a random variable in bits.
D(p‖q) = Σ p log(p/q) ≥ 0: the extra coding cost of assuming q when the truth is p; not symmetric.
I(X; Y) = H(X) − H(X | Y): how much one variable tells about another; zero exactly under independence.
P(|Xₙ − X| > ε) → 0 for every ε > 0.
P(Xₙ → X) = 1: the sequence converges for almost every outcome.
F_{Xₙ}(x) → F_X(x) at every continuity point of F_X; only the distributions converge.
If Σ P(Aₙ) < ∞, only finitely many Aₙ occur almost surely; for independent events with Σ P(Aₙ) = ∞, infinitely many occur.
Averages of i.i.d. variables with a finite mean converge to that mean (in probability for the weak law, almost surely for the strong law).
Standardised sums of i.i.d. variables with finite variance converge in distribution to the standard normal.
The CDF of a standardised sum is within C ρ/(σ³√n) of the normal CDF: the central limit theorem's rate.
Estimating an expectation, probability or integral by averaging random samples; the error falls like 1/√N.
Sampling from a proposal distribution and reweighting by the density ratio, to estimate rare-event probabilities and reduce variance.
Sampling from a distribution by running a Markov chain whose stationary distribution it is.
A random process whose next state depends only on the current one, described by a transition matrix.
The matrix P with Pᵢⱼ = P(next state j | current state i); rows sum to 1.
A distribution π with πP = π; an irreducible aperiodic finite chain converges to its unique one.
πᵢPᵢⱼ = πⱼPⱼᵢ for all states: a reversible chain, and an easy check that π is stationary.
A process formed by adding independent steps, such as ±1 with fixed probabilities.
The problem of a gambler betting until reaching 0 or a target; even a small edge against the player makes ruin likely.
A process whose expected next value, given the past, equals its current value: a fair game.
Under conditions, a martingale stopped at a stopping time has expected value equal to its starting value.
Random events in time at constant rate λ: Poisson counts in intervals and independent exponential gaps.
A Markov process in continuous time that stays in each state for an exponential time before jumping.
A continuous random process with independent normal increments, B(t) − B(s) ~ N(0, t − s); the scaling limit of random walks.
The limit of sums of squared increments over finer partitions; equal to t for Brownian motion on [0, t].
P(max_{s≤t} B(s) ≥ a) = 2P(B(t) ≥ a) for Brownian motion (and an analogue for random walks).
A rule that turns data into a guess for an unknown parameter; judged by its bias and variance.
Choosing the parameter value that maximises the probability (or density) of the observed data.
The expected curvature of the log-likelihood; its inverse bounds the variance of unbiased estimators (Cramér–Rao).
An interval produced by a procedure that covers the true parameter in a stated fraction of repeated experiments.
The distribution expressing beliefs about a parameter before seeing data.
The distribution of a parameter after the data, proportional to likelihood times prior.
A prior family for which the posterior is in the same family, such as beta for binomial data.
An interval containing the parameter with a stated posterior probability.
A collection of events closed under complements and countable unions, on which a probability measure is defined.
A triple (Ω, F, P): a sample space, a σ-algebra of events and a probability measure.
The integral built from simple functions upward that defines expectation for every kind of distribution.
The density of one measure with respect to another, dμ/dν; densities, PMFs and likelihood ratios are all of this kind.
If Xₙ → X almost surely and |Xₙ| ≤ Y with E[Y] finite, then E[Xₙ] → E[X].
If 0 ≤ Xₙ increases to X, then E[Xₙ] increases to E[X].
